transcription.tex: Complex numbers can be represented as points in a plane.\par 1. Plot a number using its real and imaginary parts.\par 2. Describe it using a distance and an angle.
3. Multiply and divide using modulus–argument form.\par 4. Interpret equations and inequalities as loci and regions.\par Angles are in radians unless stated otherwise.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Geometry behind algebra}\par For a polynomial with real coefficients, non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs. On an Argand diagram they reflect in the real axis.\par The four fourth roots of \(1+i\) lie on a circle and are separated by angles of \(\pi/2\).
The equation \(|z-1|=2\) describes a circle with centre \((1,0)\) and radius 2.\par Complex-number iteration also generates geometric patterns such as the Mandelbrot set.

transcription.tex: The complex numbers $w$ and $z$ are given by $w=k+i$ and $z=-4+5ki$, where $k$ is a real constant. Given that $\arg(w+z)=\frac{2\pi}{3}$, find the exact value of $k$.
\[\frac{1+5k}{k-4}=-\sqrt3\]\[k=\frac{4\sqrt3-1}{5+\sqrt3}\]\[=\frac{21\sqrt3-17}{22}\]This gives negative real part and positive imaginary part, as required.

transcription.tex: A complex number \(z\) is represented by the point \(P\). Given that \(|z-5-3i|=3\)\par (a) Sketch the locus of \(P\).\par (b) Find the Cartesian equation of the locus.\par (c) Find the maximum value of \(\arg z\) in the interval \((-\pi,\pi]\).\par (d) Find the minimum and maximum values of \(|z|\).
The distance from \(C=(5,3)\) is 3, so the locus is the circle of radius 3 centred at \(C\).

The largest argument occurs on the upper tangent from \(O\). At its point of contact \(T\), the radius \(CT\) is perpendicular to \(OT\). Here \(OC=\sqrt{5^2+3^2}=\sqrt{34}\).\par The real axis is the other tangent. The line \(OC\) bisects the angle between the tangents, so \(\sin\alpha=3/\sqrt{34}\) and \(\alpha\approx0.54042\). The greatest argument is \(2\alpha\approx1.081\) radians.
The nearest and farthest points lie on the line \(OC\). Subtract or add the radius: \(\min|z|=\sqrt{34}-3\), \(\max|z|=\sqrt{34}+3\).

shapes.alt: Argand axes with circle centred at C(5,3), radius 3, tangent to the real axis.
Upper tangent OT, perpendicular radius CT and the two equal half angles about OC.

transcription.tex: (a) Sketch on the same Argand diagram:\par(i) the locus of points representing $|z-2|=|z-6-8i|$\par(ii) the locus of points representing $\arg(z-4-2i)=0$\par(iii) the locus of points representing $\arg(z-4-2i)=\frac\pi2$\par(b) Shade on an Argand diagram the set of points $\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-2|\le|z-6-8i|\}\cap\{z\in\mathbb C:0\le\arg(z-4-2i)\le\frac\pi2\}$

(a) (i) The fixed points are \((2,0)\) and \((6,8)\). Their joining segment has midpoint \((4,4)\) and gradient \(8/4=2\). Its perpendicular bisector has equation \(y-4=-\tfrac12(x-4)\), or \(y=6-x/2\).\par (ii) A zero argument gives the horizontal ray \(y=2,\ x>4\).\par (iii) An argument of \(\pi/2\) gives the vertical ray \(x=4,\ y>2\).

(b) The distance inequality selects the side of the bisector containing \((2,0)\), so \(y\le6-x/2\). The angular sector gives \(x\ge4,\ y\ge2\). The boundaries meet at \((4,4)\), \((8,2)\) and \((4,2)\). Shade the triangle, omitting \((4,2)\) because its argument is undefined.

shapes.alt: Triangle bounded by x=4, y=2 and x+2y=12. The open point (4,2) is excluded.
Blank Argand axes labelled real and imaginary for the sketch.

transcription.tex: (a) Find the Cartesian equations of:\par (i) the locus of points representing \(|z+10|=|z-6-4i\sqrt2|\)\par (ii) the locus of points representing \(|z+1|=3\).\par \textbf{(b)} Find the two values of \(z\) that satisfy both \(|z+10|=|z-6-4i\sqrt2|\) and \(|z+1|=3\).\par \textbf{(c)} Hence shade in the region \(R\) on an Argand diagram which satisfies both \(|z+10|\le|z-6-4i\sqrt2|\) and \(|z+1|\le3\).

(a) (i) Put \(z=x+iy\) and square both distances.\[(x+10)^2+y^2=(x-6)^2+(y-4\sqrt2)^2.\]Cancel \(x^2+y^2\) to obtain \(32x+8\sqrt2\,y+32=0\). Hence \(y=-2\sqrt2(x+1)\).\par (ii) \(|z+1|=3\) gives \((x+1)^2+y^2=9\).

(b) Substitute the line in the circle. Then \((x+1)^2+8(x+1)^2=9\), so \(x+1=\pm1\). For \(x=0\), \(y=-2\sqrt2\). For \(x=-2\), \(y=2\sqrt2\). Thus \(z=-2\sqrt2\,i\) or \(z=-2+2\sqrt2\,i\).\par (c) The distance inequality gives \(y\le-2\sqrt2(x+1)\). Shade the part of the closed disk on that side of the line. The line passes through the centre, so the result is a semicircle with its boundary included.

shapes.alt: Closed semicircle on the lower-left side of the diameter through z=−2√2 i and z=−2+2√2 i.
Blank Argand axes labelled real and imaginary for the sketch.
